I. The Mismatch Between Human Biology and Modern Civilization

Modern societies demand sustained attention, rapid adaptation, and complex cooperative behavior on a scale our unaugmented brains and bodies struggle to manage. We see this everywhere:

  • In constant information overload that overwhelms human working memory and attention.

  • In workplaces where increasingly specialized, abstract tasks demand mental capacities that can take decades to develop, and are still prone to error, fatigue, and burnout.

Our biological design is not “bad”; it is simply obsolete relative to the world we have built. When airplanes were invented, human beings could not fly unaided. We did not lament this limit as sacred; we developed machines to extend our physical capabilities. The same logic should now be applied at a deeper level, to cognition, health, and sensory perception.

Genetic enhancement can improve baseline capacities—memory, reasoning, disease resistance, emotional regulation. Cybernetic augmentation can integrate our nervous systems directly with digital tools, granting instantaneous access to information and seamless control over machines. Together, they can realign the human organism with the environment of a high-tech civilization.

Mandatory implementation would ensure that this realignment is not a privilege of elites, but a universal condition of citizenship in a society that depends on human competence and resilience.

Societal progress is a collective phenomenon. It depends not just on a few geniuses or innovators, but on millions of competent, informed, and cooperative individuals who can understand and support complex policies. Yet our evolutionary heritage equips us with tribal instincts, myopic short-term thinking, susceptibility to misinformation, and emotional reactivity.

Cognitive and emotional enhancement can mitigate these tendencies. Imagine a population with:

  • Greater baseline empathy and emotional stability.

If a segment of the population remains easily misled, prone to panic, and cognitively overwhelmed, their choices affect public health, environmental policy, economic stability, and conflict. The benefits of enhanced reasoning and emotional maturity only fully manifest when they are shared broadly. One of the most powerful arguments for making radical human enhancement mandatory is equality.

This divide would be more profound than any existing inequality because it would be rooted in persistent biological and cognitive differences, not just social or economic circumstances. No amount of conventional education or welfare could fully close the gap between enhanced and unenhanced citizens operating in the same technological environment.

Mandatory enhancement prevents this outcome by raising the baseline for everyone. It transforms radical enhancement from a luxury into a standard, like universal literacy or public education. When everyone is enhanced:

  • Merit remains relevant, but the starting line moves up for all, reducing inherited disadvantage.

Advanced technologies bring extraordinary benefits—but also existential risks. Artificial intelligence, synthetic biology, climate engineering, and autonomous weapons demand levels of judgment, coordination, and long-term thinking that our evolved minds rarely achieve.

Autonomy is valuable, but it is not a license to endanger others or to remain permanently below the threshold of competence necessary for participating in a high-risk, high-tech society. Mandatory enhancement, properly regulated and designed to minimize harm, serves the same ethical purpose as other public safety requirements: it ensures that individuals have the capacities needed not just to protect themselves, but to avoid harming others.

Crucially, enhancement does not eliminate autonomy; it can expand it. An enhanced person has more options, greater cognitive freedom, better emotional control, and more potential life paths. The “autonomy” to remain impaired or vulnerable is a thin sort of freedom compared to the expanded autonomy that enhancement makes possible.

Another concern is that mandatory enhancement will homogenize humanity, reducing diversity and weakening the rich variation in personalities, talents, and perspectives that drive creativity.

Enhanced humans may be capable of richer diversity because more people can reach higher levels of competence, explore more domains, and experiment with a broader range of experiences.

Mandatory enhancement, carefully designed, need not flatten humanity; it can lift humanity as a whole while allowing countless ways to be uniquely human.

We have already accepted that technology should transform the environment, our tools, and our institutions. The remaining frontier is ourselves. To insist that humans remain biologically static in the face of rapidly advancing technology is to insist on a permanent, dangerous mismatch between our capabilities and our circumstances.

It is our future—if we have the courage to claim it.

As humanity stands at the precipice of unprecedented technological capability, a provocative question emerges: Should society mandate human enhancement technologies to ensure our collective survival and prosperity? Enhanced humans with improved cognitive abilities might solve these problems more effectively, while genetic modifications could provide resistance to diseases or environmental changes.

Paradoxically, mandatory enhancement advocates often invoke equality as a justification. They argue that enhancement represents a natural extension of these accepted practices—using technology to improve human wellbeing and capability at a population level.

Bodily Autonomy: The principle of informed consent and bodily autonomy stands as perhaps the strongest objection. Forcing medical procedures on unwilling individuals violates fundamental human rights principles established through centuries of ethical development.

Identity and Meaning: Many argue that fundamental human experiences and meanings might be lost if certain struggles and limitations are eliminated through enhancement.

The technical complexity, individual variation in response to treatments, and massive infrastructure required make universal mandatory enhancement logistically implausible with current or near-future technology.

The debate over mandatory human enhancement forces us to confront fundamental questions about human nature, progress, and the kind of future we want to create. From behind that veil, rational agents would unquestionably choose universal enhancement over a system in which biological augmentation is available only to the privileged.

IV. Precedent: We Already Mandate Biological Interventions

The notion of mandatory biological intervention sounds radical until we remember that we already practice it extensively and with broad public support.

Mandatory vaccination compels citizens to accept biological modification — the deliberate alteration of their immune systems — for public health. The principle is established: when individual biological status creates collective risk, the state may mandate intervention.

Mandatory education compels cognitive development for all children, overriding parental preference when necessary. We accept that the state has a legitimate interest in ensuring minimum cognitive capability. Enhancement extends this principle from environmental modification of the brain (education) to more direct methods.

Fluoride in water supplies modifies the biology of entire populations without individual consent, on the grounds that the collective dental health benefit outweighs autonomy objections.

Newborn screening and mandatory treatment for conditions like phenylketonuria already involve genetic testing and compulsory intervention to prevent cognitive disability.

Selective Service registration establishes that the state may claim the bodies of citizens for collective defense. If the state can mandate that citizens risk death in warfare, the argument that it cannot mandate cognitive or physical enhancement is difficult to sustain.

The principle underlying all these precedents is consistent: when a biological intervention produces overwhelming collective benefit, when voluntary uptake is insufficient to achieve that benefit, and when the intervention is reasonably safe, mandatory implementation is justified. Radical enhancement, once sufficiently proven, meets all three criteria.

V. The Moral Bankruptcy of Voluntariness

The strongest objection to mandatory enhancement is autonomy — the principle that individuals should control what happens to their bodies. This principle is genuinely important. But elevating it to an absolute that overrides all other considerations produces morally monstrous outcomes.

Consider: if a parent refuses to treat their child's curable cancer, we override their autonomy. If a parent refuses to educate their child, we override their autonomy. We do this because we recognize that autonomy is not the only value — that welfare, equality, and collective survival also make legitimate moral claims.

A voluntary-only enhancement framework means accepting the following:

  • Children born to anti-enhancement parents will be permanently, irremediably disadvantaged — not through any choice of their own.
  • Preventable cognitive limitations will continue to produce preventable suffering — poor decisions, addiction, inability to achieve potential.
  • Collective challenges requiring enhanced cognition will go unmet because a sufficient fraction of the population remains unenhanced.
  • Class-based speciation will proceed unchecked.

The "voluntary" framework is only voluntary for the adults making the choice. For their children, for the disadvantaged communities that predictably won't access voluntary programs, and for the species facing collective threats, it is a framework of imposed limitation.

We must be honest about what "respecting autonomy" means in this context: it means respecting the autonomy of this generation to condemn future generations to biological inadequacy. It means respecting the autonomy of the privileged to hoard enhancement while the unprivileged remain unaugmented. It means respecting individual choice over species survival.

A genuine commitment to human flourishing requires acknowledging that some enhancements — once proven safe and effective — are too important to leave to choice, just as literacy, vaccination, and basic nutrition are too important to leave to choice.

"The technology isn't ready." This is a timing objection, not a principled one. This essay argues for mandatory enhancement when the technology is sufficiently proven — establishing the ethical and policy framework now so that implementation can proceed when capability arrives. If the principle is accepted, the timeline is a technical question.

"Who decides what counts as enhancement?" Democratic institutions, guided by scientific evidence, just as they currently decide what vaccines are mandatory, what educational standards apply, and what substances are added to water supplies. The difficulty of the decision does not invalidate the principle.

"It could go wrong — unforeseen side effects." This applies to every medical intervention ever mandated. We manage this through phased rollouts, monitoring, and the same pharmacovigilance infrastructure that governs existing mandatory health interventions. The risk of enhancement must be weighed against the risk of non-enhancement — which includes existential threats, permanent inequality, and economic obsolescence.

"It violates human dignity." The concept of dignity that demands we preserve biological limitation in the face of preventable suffering and existential risk is a concept of dignity in need of revision. There is no dignity in preventable cognitive disability. There is no dignity in species extinction. True dignity lies in the capacity for flourishing — and enhancement expands that capacity.

"This is eugenics." Historical eugenics was pseudoscientific, racist, coercive in service of eliminating "undesirable" populations, and aimed at restriction rather than enhancement. Universal mandatory enhancement is the precise opposite in every dimension: scientifically grounded, universally applied regardless of race or class, and aimed at elevating all rather than eliminating some. Conflating the two is not moral seriousness — it is moral confusion that uses historical atrocity to prevent universal benefit.

The case for mandatory radical enhancement rests on a simple recognition: the challenges facing humanity in the coming century exceed the capabilities of unaugmented human biology, and a voluntary approach to overcoming those limitations will produce catastrophic inequality while leaving the species collectively unprepared.

We enhance mandatorily already — through vaccination, education, and public health infrastructure. The principle is established. What changes with genetic and cybernetic augmentation is not the principle but the magnitude of the intervention and the magnitude of the benefit.

A world of universal enhancement is a world in which every child is born free of genetic disease, every mind is equipped to comprehend the complexities of planetary stewardship, every citizen is capable of meaningful participation in an augmented economy, and the species possesses the collective cognitive capacity to navigate existential risk. A world of voluntary-only enhancement is a world of biological aristocracy, deepening inequality, and civilizational inadequacy in the face of accelerating threat.

The choice, ultimately, is between a humanity that takes active responsibility for its biological future and one that leaves that future to the lottery of birth and the marketplace of privilege. Mandatory universal enhancement is not a violation of human nature. It is human nature — the same drive that invented language, medicine, and law — carried to its logical and necessary conclusion.

The essay's strongest points are the equality argument and the precedent argument. Its weakest point is the enormous gap between principle and implementation — the governance challenges of deciding what enhancements to mandate, the genuine risk of authoritarian abuse, the difficulty of ensuring safety at population scale with novel technologies, and the deep questions about cognitive liberty and identity that even the strongest versions of this argument don't fully resolve.

The historical record of mandatory state biological programs — even well-intentioned ones — warrants genuine caution that this essay, by design, understates. The argument is strongest as a challenge to complacent voluntarism and weakest as an actual policy blueprint.

I present it not as advocacy but as an exercise in taking a radical position seriously enough to reveal both its surprising strengths and its real dangers.
